# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–34 (Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Summer of ninth year after Waterloo (1830). Chapter 34 progresses through week following Sunday, 26th April dinner. Current conversations suggest mid-to-late week.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn, Queen's Gate, Islington); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; Dunholt village; Salford; Sheepstone; Bungay; Sheep's Acre Farm; Sheepstone Birches; Yarlton; Staveton; Fenmere hill farms; Suffolk; New York; San Francisco; Liverpool; Harrowgate; Mirecombe; Duchess of Stevenage's residence; Lady Gamut's residence.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley, Mr. Osborne, Joseph Sedley, Colonel Rawdon Crawley, Sir Pitt**: All deceased as previously documented.

## Rebecca's Arc
- Never became Lady Crawley; styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) receives liberal allowance but declines to see her. Appears very wealthy at Bath and Cheltenham. Busies herself in piety and Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
- Married at Dike (Ostend); Amelia initiated encounter in "dripping white bonnet and shawl." Dobbin quit service, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane than of his History of the Punjaub.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives on Welbeck Street with Felix and Henrietta. Authored "Criminal Queens." Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer); praised by "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune. Suspects Alf orders hostile reviews of friends' works. Proposed scheme: if Henrietta married Roger, Felix could inherit his name, title, property. Felix consented to remain at Manor House. At Monday Caversham dinner, found Melmotte "heavy on her hands." Urged Felix to formally propose to Marie's father, warning: "don't put it off; you don't know how many slips there may be between the cup and the lip." Felix refused, claiming awkwardness.

**Felix Carbury**: Beautiful; cynosure of mother's eyes. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough, £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming. Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. **Sunday, 26th April: Found Madame Melmotte, Marie, Georgiana Longestaffe, and Lord Nidderdale in drawing-room. Marie fell asleep; secretly instructed Felix to find Melmotte in book-room below. Melmotte assumed Felix came about railway shares and resolved to be stern. When Melmotte questioned his income, Felix lacked courage to speak truth. Felix walked to club afterward feeling checkmated, full of wrath. After house dinner Sunday night (7 PM), approached Dolly Longestaffe for cash, urgently needing to "take up a lot of shares in the city to-morrow; or perhaps Wednesday might do," claiming Melmotte said only objection to him and Marie's marriage was money. In smoking-room, attempted business with Miles Grendall (Secretary), growing angry when Grendall remained impassive. Sunday night card-room (~11 PM): Sat next to Grendall, observed him moving chair away. Became moderate in play, almost always losing.** **Monday afternoon at club: Read Marie's letter; turned up nose, deemed much of "that kind of thing" intolerable even with marriage and money certain; crumpled letter muttering "What an infernal little ass!"** **Chapter 34—Mid-week: Spent two days in unendurable idleness. Referred to money Dolly owed him, explaining commercial arrangement would be serviceable; particularly anxious to take up railway shares. Later told Dolly he would dine at club but could not stay for whist afterward, declaring he could not stay at club with "considerable mystery in his manner." Acceded willingly to Dolly's plan visiting Abchurch Lane following day; after negotiation, agreed to meet at 2 P.M. at club (Dolly had suggested 4 P.M., Felix had proposed noon; split difference). Dined with Dolly; Miles Grendall dining alone at next table; Felix did not join Dolly and Grendall's conversation, nor did Grendall address Felix. When Dolly asked "Is there anything up between you and Miles?" Felix paused and said "No;--that is not the reason. I'll tell you all about it in the cab to-morrow." Left club, declared intention to visit Marie Melmotte at Grosvenor Square, but did not go in upon arrival—questioning what good it would do until he got Melmotte's consent and money to buy shares. Evening activities unspecified. Upon returning home at early hour, found note from Marie.**

**Marie Melmotte to Felix** (letter Sunday evening): "Papa is very cross to her [mamma] sometimes...if he does [beat me], I'll bear it,—for your sake...I will never,--never give you up...Do write and tell me that you love me...You can come and call,--unless papa tells the man in the hall not to let you in...Papa dined out yesterday with that Lord Alfred, so I haven't seen him since you were here."

**Marie's Note to Felix** (mid-week, Chapter 34): "Why don't we see you? Mamma would say nothing if you came. Papa is never in the drawing-room. Miss Longestaffe is here of course, and people always come in in the evening. We are just going to dine out at the Duchess of Stevenage's. Papa, and mamma and I. Mamma told me that Lord Nidderdale is to be there, but you need not be a bit afraid. I don't like Lord Nidderdale, and I will never take any one but the man I love. You know who that is. Miss Longestaffe is so angry because she can't go with us. What do you think of her telling me that she did not understand being left alone? We are to go afterwards to a musical party at Lady Gamut's. Miss Longestaffe is going with us, but she says that she hates music. She is such a set-up thing! I wonder why papa has her here. We don't go anywhere to-morrow evening, so pray come."

**Henrietta Carbury**: Rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable. Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," promising not to see her three months. Wore rose from Roger's room. When met Roger at door, there was "more in her eyes of graciousness towards him than he had ever seen there before." Roger declared love anew (Chapter 32 evening); Henrietta has not committed; Roger's determination remains unshaken. Paul Montague is thoroughly in love with her.

## Ruby Ruggles
- Granddaughter of old Daniel Ruggles, of Sheep's Acre, parish of Sheepstone, near Bungay. Pretty with long glossy ringlets, large round dark eyes, clear dark complexion; strong, healthy, tall; possessed own will. Had been to marry John Crumb (marriage abandoned/postponed). Understood degradation must be avoided. After Sunday meeting with Felix, resolved: "I suppose I am to be his wedded wife...I'll never be nothing unless I'm that."

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company. Arrived London from Paris within two years; claims English birth but speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair; expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. In City, his name "worth any money." Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs; has Caversham and Sussex property. Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary. **By Chapter 33 Board day, has twice sold fifty shares at £112 10s., receiving cheques for £625 each (£25 profit per share above £100 nominal). During Whitsun week country visit, remained in summer-house with Lord Alfred, smoking, drinking brandy and seltzer, appearing not in good humour. Chapter 34: Is negotiating to purchase Pickering property from Sir Merton Longestaffe.** **Believed by Montague to be "as vile a scoundrel as ever lived."**

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well; has begun forming own opinions. Rejected Lord Grasslough; has experience with Lord Nidderdale. Currently pursued by Sir Felix Carbury (claimed favourite in London). **Sunday: Fell asleep in chair before fire. Secretly instructed Felix to find father in book-room. Resolved on constancy toward Felix; rejected other suitors. Felt complete happiness; promised to tell mother. Chapter 34: Staying with parents in Grosvenor Square. Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner and Lady Gamut's musical party (evening); family will have no engagement next evening. Sent mid-week note to Felix expressing that she will never take anyone but man she loves (Felix); hopes he will call when family is out or when people call in evenings. Notes Miss Longestaffe's presence and anger at not attending parties.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Gracious as usual but never very gracious. Called Miss Longestaffe "a great bore" and "fatigante." Dismissed Marie's declarations of caring. Appears to know of Felix's offer; does not absolutely disapprove. In Chapter 34, present at Grosvenor Square with Marie and Georgiana Longestaffe; attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner.

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Determined no more London expenses that year; family will not return from Caversham. Desires to sell Pickering and disembarrass Caversham from debt. Dolly refused to consent unless half produce given to him. Broke promise to Georgiana of returning to London. **Chapter 34: Received letter (from Dolly) like a thunderbolt that Melmottes must be "very bad indeed,--worse than he had thought." Most angered by passage telling him he ought to have taken family back to town—from his son who had refused to help him in his difficulties. Is negotiating sale of Pickering to Melmotte.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe**: Made strong protest against Melmottes; threatened to stay in London. Father refused; she felt "treachery." Meditated revenge: "I will do something. I'm not going to be cheated and swindled." Following morning, Lady Pomona handed her undated invitation from Melmotte to stay with them. Questioned mother. Expressed contempt for Melmottes, calling them vulgar. Yet concluded: "I'll go." **Friday morning before departure to railway station, conversation with younger sister Sophia was "almost touching." Georgiana failed to hold up her head as usual; cowed.** **By Sunday, present at Grosvenor Square drawing-room with Madame Melmotte, Marie, and Lord Nidderdale, carrying on flirtation with Nidderdale in half whisper, wholly indifferent to hostess or young lady of house.** **Chapter 34: Now staying with Melmottes in Grosvenor Square. Dependent on Madame Melmotte for carriage outings and access to social parties. Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner and Lady Gamut's musical party. Angry at being left alone by family; tells Marie she does not understand being left alone. Hates music.**

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe**: Has own rooms in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Obdurate regarding his own rights in property dealings. **Chapter 34: Called on his sister at Melmotte house—came very early hour, not much after noon (unusual for him). Georgiana complained of confinement. Within last half hour received letter from lawyer regarding Pickering sale negotiations. States his governor wants to sell Pickering; Melmotte wants to buy. His father cannot sell without his consent. Has asked for half the plunder (over and above £50,000 price, above debt on property); £25,000 would pay off what he owes on his own property and make him "very square." Expects father to give in to his terms. Expressed reluctance about property going to pieces, saying "A fellow oughtn't to let his family property go to pieces," though acknowledges property gives only 3 per cent. while borrowed money costs 6 per cent. to governor and 25 per cent. to himself. Property should be sold. States Melmotte knows all about it; offers to go with Felix to city to-morrow and make it straight about what Felix owes him. Says Melmotte will advance him £1,000, allowing Felix to get railway shares. Mid-week: Dined with Felix at Beargarden; Miles Grendall dining alone at next table; spoke frequently with Grendall but Felix would not join conversation. In smoking-room afterward, asked Felix "Is there anything up between you and Miles?" Felix said no and promised to tell him "all about it in the cab to-morrow." Agreed with Felix on plan to visit Abchurch Lane next day; after negotiation, settled on 2 P.M. departure time from club.**

**Lady Pomona**: Complained of headache at Caversham; slept through afternoon's tension. Gave Georgiana Melmotte's invitation. Attending Duchess of Stevenage's dinner.

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Approximately 2,000 miles. Fisker considers cost questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway.

**London Directorate**: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (MP for Staines), Lord Nidderdale, Paul Montague.

**Fisker's Departure**: Started Saturday morning, 19th April. Met by Nidderdale and Montague.

## Paul Montague and Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle

**Paul's Situation**: Living at Beargarden. Junior member of railway firm; English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination. Trembles for his money. Entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte in Grosvenor Square. Saw good deal of Sir Felix, Lord Nidderdale; champagne consumption increased. **Sunday night card-room: Present at gambling; won heavily from him by Grendall in run of luck.** **Thoroughly in love with Hetta Carbury; not in love with Mrs. Hurtle. Would have given much of his golden prospects in American railway to have Mrs. Hurtle "reconveyed suddenly to San Francisco." Yet he has delight in her presence. Of natural disposition to have strongest affinities and sympathies with women; rarely altogether happy when removed from their influence.** No other friend in whom he can confide; only Hetta herself. Considered writing stern letter telling her marriage impossible, but remembered her solitude, her picture of herself in London without acquaintance except himself; convinced himself he cannot leave her without seeing her.

**Mrs. Winifrid Hurtle**: Formerly betrothed to Paul. Arrived night before last (Tuesday reached Liverpool, came to London Wednesday). During earlier engagement, he told her he was "going to see what he could make of his broken fortunes" and she promised to follow him. He saw her in New York on second journey to San Francisco, renewed promises despite cousin's caution. Since then never met until Chapter 34. She had not made promised journey to San Francisco before he left it. Letters from her reached him in England; he answered explaining engagement must end. Has now followed him to London. She said: "I could not get across to San Francisco as I said I would, and when I was there you had quarrelled with your uncle and returned." When he told her "Things are changed," she threw herself on knees: "Paul, I have come again across the Atlantic on purpose to see you,--after so many months,--and will you not give me one kiss?" He kissed her, embraced her warmly, wished she had remained away but could not refuse her. She said: "I at any rate have been faithful."

**Mrs. Hurtle's Letters and Demands**: She writes that his love is everything to her; she abandoned friends and devoted herself wholly to him. She scorns to supplicate but demands he hear her. She acknowledges he loves Henrietta Carbury ("the other—nameless lady"), but insists he once loved her and could love her again. She appeals: "You sin against me to my utter destruction if you leave me. I have given up every friend I have to follow you." She fought legal battle over her property in California and won it, "forced to fight a battle about my property, and I have won it...at the teeth of robbers." She will not plead as pauper. Cruel rumours have followed her regarding late husband and concerning Paul; these have been said to others. She has come alone to England without introductions or friends, driven by need to see him and hear her fate. She appeals: "Let me see you as I used to see you, and let me be seen as I used to be seen." She requests he dine with her and take her to theatre, promising not to allude to his revelation about Henrietta unless he wishes.

**Theatre Evening**: Paul took Mrs. Hurtle to theatre. She commented on acting: "The acting isn't very good." Spoke of how little that is "really jolly" exists. Addressed play's portrayal of woman crying because lover talked to another woman: "What I find fault with is that the writers and actors are so ignorant of men and women as we see them every day. It's all right that she should cry, but she shouldn't cry there." She noted position described was nearly her own; spoke "on purpose,--fighting her own battle after her own fashion, knowing well that her words would confuse him." Instructed that women hide such tears—"A woman hides such tears. She may be found crying because she is unable to hide them;--but she does not willingly let the other woman see them. Does she?" After theatre, said regarding cab ride to Islington: "You need not. I'm not a bit afraid of a London cab by myself." But of course Paul accompanied her to Islington. She continued talking during whole journey. Remarked on London's immensity and dirt; compared New York (bigger than Paris but pleasanter). Called Paris "gem of gems among towns." Stated she did not like Frenchmen, liked Englishmen better than Americans, but fancied could never like English women. "I do so hate all kinds of buckram. I like good conduct, and law, and religion too if it be not forced down one's throat; but I hate what your women call propriety. I suppose what we have been doing to-night is very improper; but I am quite sure that it has not been in the least wicked." She thinks in solitude: "He should marry her,--or there should be something done which should make the name of Winifrid Hurtle known to the world! She had no plan of revenge yet formed. She would not talk of revenge,--she told herself that she would not even think of revenge,--till she was quite sure that revenge would be necessary. But she did think of it, and could not keep her thoughts from it for a moment." Questions whether he, greatly inferior to herself intellectually and in person, should throw her over. Believes he promised to marry her: "He had promised to marry her; and he should marry her, or the world should hear the story of his perjury!"

**Montague's Dilemma**: Feels surrounded by difficulties upon reading Hurtle's letters. Heart is "all the other way" (toward Henrietta), but no escape seems open. Had resolved to break his word before seeing Henrietta, believing Roger Carbury's warnings that marriage to mysterious American adventuress would be ruin—"Any scrape is better than that scrape." All San Francisco reports substantiated Roger's views; woman might never have had husband, might have two or three, might be overwhelmed with debt, might be anything abominable. Believed Roger with double faith upon seeing Henrietta. Yet every word of Hurtle's letter is uncontradictable; he had loved her, promised marriage, and determined to break word. Cannot go to Roger for advice, as Roger is his rival for Henrietta. Roger's honesty would prevent self-interested counsel, but Paul cannot speak of Henrietta to his rival. As evening approaches, he dreads parting with her and making arrangements for future meeting. Knows he is in great peril but does not know how to escape.

## Lord Nidderdale
Intent on marrying Marie Melmotte for her fortune. Claims not afraid of Melmotte, believing Melmotte "rather likes me, because I've always been on the square with him," asserting "If it depended on him, you know, I should have the girl to-morrow." On Friday Board day, walked with Melmotte to Abchurch Lane offices, asking about his position regarding shares. Melmotte told him to wait, shares would be allocated but not transferable until he qualifies by investing "a few thousand pounds." **Sunday drawing-room: Flirting with Miss Longestaffe in half whisper, wholly indifferent to hostess or young lady of house. Sunday night: Present at card-room gambling; objected to loo but capitulated. Chapter 34: To be at Duchess of Stevenage's dinner; Marie's mother warned her that he would be there, but Marie has expressed that she does not like him and will never take anyone but man she loves.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile." Took degree at Oxford; became "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning day-labourer's wages; forced to buy second-hand clothes. Soft heart; knows Lady Carbury false and Felix worthless, yet condemns himself for harsh words. During Sunday evening with Father Barham, engaged in theological debate; became tired of priest's intolerance. Later showed courtesy as host despite disapproval of Melmotte scheme. Declared love to Henrietta anew (Chapter 32 evening); determination remains unshaken. Is rival for Henrietta's affection with Paul Montague.

## Father John Barham
Priest of Beccles. Dogmatic Catholic; believes man should abandon reason to care of another or others. Faith sufficient unto itself. In county only twelve months; knew nearly every Roman Catholic's name within borders.

## Property Relations
**Daniel Ruggles' Land**: Holds Sheep's Acre Farm on bishop's lease, part of property which belonged to bishopric of Elmham. Also holds small extent of outlying meadow belonging to Carbury estate; thus one of Roger Carbury's tenants. Sheepstone Birches (wood/copse) belonged to Roger.

## Other Characters
- **Miles Grendall**: Secretary/usher to Melmotte. Does not pay debts of honour; made no answer regarding repayment; lacks impudence to avoid discussing business while accepting that private matters separate from affairs of business. **Sunday card-room: Won heavily, particularly from Paul Montague; destroyed paper counters representing £1,000+; received considerable ready money "quite a godsend to him." When pressed by Felix about debt, rose and suggested billiards, walking slowly out of room, leaving Felix to take what revenge he pleased. Felix feared Grendall was more popular man than himself and did not expose transaction to whole room. During hour of play, observed moving chair farther from Felix and nearer to Dolly. Chapter 34: Mid-week at Beargarden, dined alone at table next to Felix and Dolly; spoke frequently with Dolly but never addressed Felix, nor did Felix join conversation; Dolly noticed distance.**
- **Lord Grasslough**: Present at Sunday card-room gambling.
